scene.testo: "Hitler is dead." That was her entire reply to the American captain who asked whether the Führer had survived. Five months after Berlin fell, one of the last people to leave his bunker said it. The record holds it.

Why would an American officer even ask? Because in the autumn of 1945, rumors claimed Hitler had escaped and was hiding in the mountains of Austria. And the woman across the table had landed in exactly those mountains.
Her name was Hanna Reitsch. She had flown into a burning Berlin to reach Hitler. But the real question is not what she said. It is why the Americans doubted her, and why her words held.

The setting was Austria, 1945. The man holding the pen was Captain Robert Work of the Army Air Forces, an interrogator with the Air Interrogation Unit. His report on her statements is dated October 8, 1945, and marked confidential.

Across Europe, Hitler's pilots, generals, and secretaries were being questioned. The Allies wanted facts, not legends. Reitsch mattered because she had been inside the bunker during the final week, and few other survivors had seen him that late.

Hanna Reitsch was thirty-three years old. She was a test pilot who had flown gliders, jets, and rocket planes, and she was the first woman to fly a helicopter. Few people in Germany knew aircraft better.
She wore the Iron Cross, First Class, and she had stayed loyal to the regime to the very end. That matters. A hostile witness might lie to hurt Hitler. A loyal one had little reason to call him dead.

To understand her answer, go back to April 1945. Soviet armies were closing around Berlin. On April 24, Hitler summoned General Robert Ritter von Greim from Bavaria and ordered him to report to the capital at once.

Greim took Reitsch along as his pilot. They flew from Rechlin toward Berlin with fighter escorts, landing at Gatow, the last airfield in German hands. Soviet aircraft were strafing it as they touched down.

The telephone lines to the Chancellery were dead. So Greim took a small Fieseler Storch and flew toward the center of the city at treetop height, with Reitsch aboard. Antiaircraft fire tore into the plane.

A bullet shattered Greim's right foot. Reitsch reached over, took the controls, and set the Storch down on the broad avenue near the Brandenburg Gate. It was April 26. Within hours, they stood inside Hitler's bunker.

Hitler had called Greim for one reason. Hermann Göring had radioed that he was ready to take over the Reich. Hitler called it treason, stripped Göring of his offices, and named Greim commander of the Luftwaffe.

That first evening, Reitsch later said, Hitler handed her two small vials of poison. Everyone around him carried one, she told Work, and each person was responsible for leaving no recognizable body behind.

She asked why he stayed. His answer, as she told it, was hope. An army under General Walther Wenck, he said, would drive the Russians back from the south. But his face, she told Work, said the war was lost.

Over the next days she watched him closely. He paced the bunker with a street map of Berlin, moving markers for armies that were too weak to reach him. Wenck's forces had no chance of breaking through.

In her account, the defense of Berlin was chaos. There was no clear plan, no working radio link to the fighting units, and almost no information. Orders traveled by messenger and by one telephone line to a flak tower.

On April 28, word arrived that Heinrich Himmler had tried to open surrender talks with the Western Allies through Count Folke Bernadotte of Sweden. Hitler's rage, Reitsch said, was beyond anything she had ever seen.

Hitler wanted Himmler stopped. He also wanted every available aircraft thrown against the Soviet forces nearing the Chancellery. Only Greim could issue those orders, and only if he got out of the bunker alive.

So Hitler ordered them to leave. Reitsch begged to stay. According to her, he refused, and the two pilots prepared to leave the shelter for a city under fire. Their wounded general limped on a shattered foot.
They climbed out into streets lit by fire. A small Arado trainer had been readied near the Brandenburg Gate. Reitsch flew it off a stretch of road under searchlights and shellfire, and turned north.
She was convinced hers was the last aircraft to leave Berlin. Other planes sent in afterward, she said, were shot down. The Russians, she told Work, already held a solid ring around the city.

Hitler stayed behind. Allied investigators later established that he shot himself on April 30 in the Chancellery bunker, and that Eva Braun died beside him. Reitsch was gone before it happened, but she had seen his last days.
Now the captain's question made sense. Reitsch and Greim had ended the war in the Tyrol. They flew to Zell am See, then on to Kitzbühel, and surrendered to American forces there in May 1945.
To investigators, the pattern looked suspicious. The pilot who flew out of Hitler's bunker lands where the rumor placed him. If anyone knew of a secret escape, it might be her. Work had to ask.
Work noted that she was visibly distressed that anyone would suggest it. Then came her answer, short and flat. The report records it with no argument and no explanation. "Hitler is dead."
She did not stop there. The man she saw in the shelter, she said, could not have lived on. He had lost every reason to live, and he knew it better than anyone.
Even if a path to freedom had been cleared for him, she told the captain, he lacked the strength to use it. Hitler, she insisted, never left Berlin. No plane, she said, ever carried him out.
Work did not treat her as flawless. He wrote that her quotations were not exact, only as she remembered them. She was unsure about names and times, and he said so in the report.

One of her certainties was plainly wrong. She called the idea of a wedding in the bunker almost ludicrous. In fact, Hitler married Eva Braun there in the early hours of April 29, while Greim was still inside.

Why did her answer matter? Because rumors of a surviving Führer were a political danger. Allied officials feared a hidden-Hitler myth could encourage die-hard followers and complicate the occupation of Germany. Every credible witness narrowed the room for it.

Her account also fit other evidence. Witnesses from the bunker, questioned separately, described the same final days, and in the months ahead British investigators gathered testimony that Hitler died on April 30 in the Chancellery grounds.
Her words also showed a witness losing faith. According to Work, she called Hitler a criminal against the world, and said such power must never again rest in the hands of one man.
By then her own world had collapsed. Greim was in American custody. On May 24, 1945, he killed himself with poison in Salzburg. Work wrote that Reitsch had been seriously tempted to do the same.
She told the captain she lived only to tell the truth: about the bunker, about Hitler, and about the system that had led Germans there. Whether she told all of it is another question.

Later she disputed parts of the report, saying she had been misquoted. But the record remains: a confidential file typed in Austria in October 1945, and an answer that matched the later findings about Hitler's death.

Hitler had not hidden in the Tyrol. He had died in Berlin, and the pilot who flew out of that burning city said so plainly. Subscribe, and tell us in the comments whose interrogation we should open next.

descrizione:
In the autumn of 1945, an American interrogator in Austria asked Hanna Reitsch, one of the last people to leave Hitler's bunker, whether the Führer had survived. Her reply was short and unambiguous, and it is still in the confidential report.

This documentary follows her flight into besieged Berlin, her days inside the Führerbunker, Hitler's final orders, and the interrogation by Captain Robert Work of the Army Air Forces. It also covers the flaws in her account and why it mattered to the Allies in 1945.

Based on Allied interrogation records and documented World War II history. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more first-hand accounts from the archives.
